greet.text: He is mending a rope that does not need mending, which is what a man does when he is deciding whether to like you. The boat behind him is hauled up and leaking at a seam he has not caulked. "You want the island. Everyone wants the island, and the island does not want any of us."

choices.text: I can work aboard, if there is work.

again.text: "The mole is still there. So is the price." He does not look up from the rope. The splice in his hands is neat and old, and he is undoing it. "Say what you came to say before the wind turns."

again-booked.text:
"The mole before the gulls," he says, before you can ask. "The boat has not gone, and the price has not changed."

He spits over the side and watches the water take it. "When you are ready to sail, you sail. I am not your father and I will not wait on your breakfast."

choices.text: I can work aboard again if you need hands.
choices.unavailableNote: You have no Akkadian to offer him, and a master will not shout the terms twice.

sailing.text:
"When you have the fare and your cargo is on the mole. The boat is not waiting on the wind; it is waiting on you."

He goes back to the rope, then says, to the rope: "The last man who made me wait paid me in a story about a storm. I have enough storms."

price.text: "**Eight if we hug the shore** and sleep on the boat. **Fourteen if we go straight across** and sleep when we get there. Neither price includes your cargo, and both include my opinion." He names the sums the way a man names his children, in order, without affection.

choices.text: I would sooner work aboard than sit idle.
choices.unavailableNote: You cannot argue terms in a language you do not have.

work.text:
"Then be at **the mole before the gulls**. Do not bring more than you can carry up a gangplank in the dark. It will not pay your passage; the fare is still the fare. But a man who works is easier to take than one who does not."

He turns away before you can agree, which is how a bargain is closed here. Then, because he cannot help it: "And **bring your own bread**. The crew is owed wages and I will not have them watching you eat."

provenance.notes: Tiro and his fares are invented; passage by fare or by work is a plausible arrangement.

scene.goal: Book passage without paying more than the fare
scene.obstacle: A leaking hull and a crew owed wages
scene.turn: He offers work instead of charity
